findings.title: BSD sed -i requires an explicit backup suffix
findings.claim: On macOS, `sed -i` without an argument consumes the next token as the backup suffix, so `sed -i s/a/b/ file` silently treats the expression as the suffix and fails, unlike GNU sed where -i takes no argument.
findings.appliesTo: macOS and other BSD userlands, where sed is not GNU sed.
findings.expectation: A script using `sed -i` that works on Linux CI works on a developer laptop.
findings.reality: BSD sed reads the next token as the backup suffix. The script fails, or worse, edits the wrong path. Scripts written on Linux break only on macOS, and vice versa.
findings.mechanism: BSD sed defines -i as taking a mandatory extension argument; GNU sed defines it as optional.
findings.workaround: Use `sed -i '' -e expr file` on BSD and `sed -i -e expr file` on GNU, or avoid in-place editing in portable scripts entirely.

findings.title: Case-insensitive filesystems make two distinct git paths collide
findings.claim: On a default macOS volume the filesystem is case-insensitive, so a repository containing both Foo.ts and foo.ts checks out only one of them and reports the other as deleted.
findings.appliesTo: Default APFS and HFS+ volumes on macOS, and Windows NTFS by default.
findings.expectation: A clean clone of a repository produces a clean working tree.
findings.reality: git status reports a deletion nobody made, and the deletion reappears after every checkout. Committing the apparent fix deletes the file for contributors on case-sensitive systems.
findings.mechanism: Git tracks paths as bytes; the filesystem folds case. Two index entries map to one directory entry.
findings.workaround: Rename one path so the pair no longer collides, or work from a case-sensitive volume. Never resolve it by committing the phantom deletion.
